dataset.name: Demographic data of Sedum lanceolatum from 2013 to 2014 under a climate manipulation experiment
description: Demographic data of Sedum lanceolatum under a climate manipulation experiment (heating and watering). Dataset includes one .csv with demographic data for 232 individuals monitored over 2013-2014 which was used, in part, to draw conclusions in "Elevation effects on vital rate sensitivities generate variation in neighbor effects on population growth rate in Sedum lanceolatum" by Herzog et al. (in review). All data was collected under a watering and warming experiment as part of the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment at Niwot Ridge, Colorado, USA. There are two main data file formats in this archive: comma-separated values (.csv) which can be read using any simple text editor program, such as TextEdit (Mac) and Notepad (Windows). The .pdf data user’s guide can be read using Adobe Acrobat Reader, or any other compatible software.
keywords: EARTH SCIENCE > CLIMATE INDICATORS > CLIMATE FEEDBACKS

spatialCoverage.description: Data used in this experiment were collected from plots set up as part of the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment (ATWE), located on Niwot Ridge in the Front Range of the Colorado Rocky Mountains, USA. A total of three experimental sites were set up as part of ATWE, but only the alpine site was used for this publication.

measurementTechnique: We collected demographic data within the ATWE experiment, a heating and watering experiment at Niwot Ridge Long-Term Ecological Research site to isolate the climatic drivers of vital rate variation across elevations. The ATWE experiment consisted of replicated factorial manipulations of heating and watering at three sites; we worked at the “Alpine” site (40° 3’16” N, 105° 35’37” W, 3540 m), similar in elevation to our high elevation populations described in the previous sections (Fig. 1 in publication). At this site in 2008, twenty 3m diameter plots were assigned to one of four treatments: 1) an unmanipulated control; 2) heated; 3) watered; or 4) heated and watered (hereafter, “heated + watered”). Heating, begun in 2009, was accomplished with active infrared heaters and increased soil temperatures by ~1.5° C at 5-10 cm soil depth during the snow-free season (Jabis et al., 2020), approximately half the difference in temperature between our low and high elevation sites during the growing season (Supp. Tables 1 and 2). Watering, begun in 2010, was accomplished by weekly hand watering of 2.5 mm of water and increased local June-September precipitation by approximately 20% of 1951-1980 mean annual precipitation of the site (Jabis et al., 2020). We used species composition studies in these plots, collected between 2009-2012 as part of the ATWE experiment (Winkler, Chapin, & Kueppers, 2016) to identify plots in which S. lanceolatum was present.

To quantify heating and watering effects on S. lanceolatum, starting in 2012 we conducted demographic censuses in plots in which S. lanceolatum was or had been present in 2009-2012. Namely, if S. lanceolatum was recorded in a plot sometime between 2009-2012, we randomly selected a 50x50 cm subset of the plot in which to search exhaustively for all S. lanceolatum individuals. If that subset did not contain S. lanceolatum, we randomly selected another subset of the plot until we found a subset that did contain S. lanceolatum. In each of those subsets, during peak fruiting in early Fall 2013, we marked and mapped all S. lanceolatum individuals, measuring size and counting fruits. In total, we measured 231 individuals across 15 plots. We returned in 2014 during peak fruiting to score survival, measure size, and count fruits. We used these data to estimate the same five size-dependent vital rates described in the prior section, though we did not separately estimate seedlings per fruit. Hereafter, we call data collected at ATWE “climate experiment data.”

We used a model selection approach (Bartoń, 2020) to assess the impacts of climate on S. lanceolatum vital rates. We compared subsets of a global linear model that contained fixed effects of log-transformed size and two categorical terms heating and watering (note heating+watering climate treatment data was coded as both heating and watering). we used mixed linear models for the likelihood of fruiting, conditional number of fruits (i.e., if fruiting occurs, the number of fruits produced), growth, and variance in growth to account for a random effect of plot. We used AICc (Hurvich & Tsai, 1989) to select a best-fit model.

We then used these best-fit models to create an integral projection model (IPM; Easterling, Ellner, and Dixon (2000)) for each of our two climate treatments, which we used to estimate deterministic population growth rate. We incorporated parameter uncertainty in the fixed effect estimates by sampling 500 sets of parameter estimates from a multivariate normal distribution parametrized using the variance-covariance matrix of fixed effect coefficients. We present 95% confidence intervals calculated across these 500 replicates. Our discretized IPM had 100 meshpoints and used log-transformed size as a response variable. To handle eviction problems, we renormalized transition probabilities to fit within the confines of the matrix (Williams, Miller, & Ellner, 2012). Seedlings enter the kernel with a mean size reflective of all observed seedlings across all populations (we had insufficient data to estimate variance in seedling size). We estimate climate treatment effects on population growth rate as the difference between deterministic growth rate in control vs. heating (or vs. watering, or vs. heating + watering). For these IPMs, we use estimates of seedlings per fruit from the high elevation demography data and seedling mean size reflective of the demography data.
